text: Τὸν παρόντα τῶν σκαμμάτων αἰῶνα. Quod in Pico exstat, præsens scenæ sæculum, typographicum mendum puto, ac eum arenæ scripsisse, quam et ego vocem, Græcæ vocis explicandæ causa adjeci. Utraque enim idem utrisque significatur locus certaminis ac fossa, in qua non esset ejus defugere aleam, sed vel cum adversario pugile decertandum, vel cum bestiis depugnandum, in quibus tale certamen gentilium feritate exhibebatur ; quod nihil cum scena, ut liquet, habet commune. Quod vero sequitur, ὅλοι ὅλῳ Θεῷ ἐγκραθῆναι, toti in toto Deo firmari, id vero ipsius Pici inscitiæ, dum non advertit τὸ, κραθεὶς et ἐγκραθεὶς, ἀπὸ τοῦ κεράννυμι esse, miscere, qua voce intima illa mentis cum Deo unio passim theologis significatur.
anchorLine: παρόντα τῶν σκαμμάτων αἰῶνα (m) διέβησαν· τὴν
en: 'The present age of the σκάμματα' (the wrestling-pits). What stands in Picus, 'the present age of the stage', I take to be a printer's error, and that he wrote 'of the arena' (arenæ), a word I too added to explain the Greek word. For both words signify the same thing, the place of contest, the pit in which one could not shirk the hazard, but must fight either with an adversary as boxer or struggle with wild beasts, in which such combat was displayed with the savagery of the heathen; which, as is clear, has nothing in common with the stage. As to what follows, 'ὅλοι ὅλῳ Θεῷ ἐγκραθῆναι', which Picus renders 'to be made firm, all in the whole God', that is Picus's own ignorance, since he does not notice that κραθείς and ἐγκραθείς come from κεράννυμι, 'to mix', the word by which the mind's inmost union with God is everywhere signified by theologians.

text: Ἐνέργειαν δὲ, τὸ νόημα. Varia ejus vocis acceptio, sæpius Maximo discussa ; ea occasione, quod pro ipsa operatione vel facultate, una in Christo asserebatur, his qui proxime Eutychiano errori accedebant, qua ἀνενέργητον humanam in Christo naturam ponebant, ipsam tollentes, siquidem nihil in natura est, non naturali præditum facultate. Hic ἐνέργειαν, ipsum dicit intellectionis terminum ac verbum, in quo mens rem intueretur. Anastasiam exponit Maximus, dum unam ipse videtur velle ἐνέργειαν, pro effectu, in his quæ ex Vaticanis codd. ejus argumenti damus.
unreadable: in the words 'Anastasiam' and 'Vaticanis' a letter or two is worn on the plate; read as printed above
anchorLine: ἐνέργειαν δὲ, τὸ νόημα (n). Πέρας γὰρ τοῦτο,
en: 'And operation (energeia) is the thought.' The varied acceptation of this word, often discussed by Maximus; on the occasion that 'one operation' or faculty was asserted in Christ by those who came closest to the Eutychian error, who posited a human nature in Christ that was 'without operation' (ἀνενέργητον), thereby removing it, since nothing in nature exists that is not endowed with a natural faculty. Here he calls the 'energeia' itself the term and word of intellection, in which the mind looks at a thing. Maximus explains Anastasius (his 'one energeia') as meaning 'by effect', in the passages from the Vatican codices that we give on that subject.

text: Ἀνεκφοίτητος ἑαυτοῦ. Sic omnino leg. pro eo quod erat, ἀνεκφοίτητον : quam vocem male Picus active reddit, refertque ad δύναμιν, et nunquam deserentem ; cum referat ipsum Deum. Nihil communius in theologia, quam divinas processiones ἀνεκφοιτήτως intelligendas esse ; ita ut per eas personæ (vel ipsa Trinitas in processionibus ad extra) non a se exeant producendo, etsi vere in iis quæ producta sunt, vel personis vel rebus, vere exsistant. Aliter tamen personæ in personis ; aliter Trinitas in rebus, de quibus hic loquitur Maximus : Τὸ, πολὺν τὸν εἰς τὰ ὄντα ἀγαθὸν ἔρωτα : inscite idem, summum erga creaturas bonum amorem. Prima ratio est cur Deus zelotes, quod vi maxima boni amoris erga res præditus sit : est enim zelus, amoris excessus. Erudita Maximo omnia
unreadable: the Greek words inside the note are worn (ἀνεκφοίτητον, ἀνεκφοιτήτως, πολὺν τὸν εἰς τὰ ὄντα ἀγαθὸν ἔρωτα) and are given as read; 'cendum' at the start of the next page's Latin column is unrelated
anchorLine: ἐκστατικὴν ὑπερούσιον δύναμιν, ἀνεκφοίτητος ἑαυτοῦ (o). Διὸ καὶ ζηλωτήν
en: 'Unforthcoming from himself' (ἀνεκφοίτητος ἑαυτοῦ). Read thus entirely, in place of what stood (ἀνεκφοίτητον): a word Picus wrongly renders actively and refers to power, 'and never deserting', whereas it refers to God himself. Nothing is more usual in theology than that the divine processions are to be understood as 'not going forth' (ἀνεκφοιτήτως): so that through them the persons (or the Trinity itself in the processions outward) do not leave themselves by producing, even though they truly exist in what is produced, whether persons or things; yet otherwise persons in persons, otherwise the Trinity in things, of which Maximus here speaks: 'the abundant love of the good toward beings' (Picus ineptly: 'the highest love of good toward creatures'). The first reason why God is a jealous one is that he is endowed with the greatest force of good love toward things: for jealousy (zelus) is excess of love. Maximus has [all] learning on these [matters] [the note continues in the right column].

text: Ἁπλῆ καὶ ἀκίνητος. Lego quod in Schol. ad Dionysium habetur et in ipso Dionysio, αὐτοκίνητος : explicatur enim divinus in seipso et ad seipsum amoris motus, cujus simulacrum sit nostra in ipsum ἀεικίνητος ἔφεσις : jugis motus appetitus. Quod sic auguste Maximus, Ἡ ἐρωτικὴ κίνησις τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ προϋπάρχουσα ἐν τῷ ἀγαθῷ : Amoris motus erga bonum ipse prior exsistens in bono ; in Deo scilicet quasi in exemplari, qui est ipsum bonum amans, seque adeo bonum amans, ex quo omnis origo amoris boni. Illepide Picus : Motus qui est in primis amans boni, etc.
anchorLine: ἁπλῆ καὶ ἀκίνητος (p)**οὖσα, καὶ
en: 'Simple and unmoved.' I read what is found in the scholia to Dionysius and in Dionysius himself: αὐτοκίνητος ('self-moved'), for what is explained is the divine motion of love in himself and toward himself, whose likeness is our ever-moving (ἀεικίνητος) yearning toward him, a constant motion of desire. This Maximus says grandly: 'the erotic motion of the good, pre-existing in the good': the motion of love toward the good, itself prior and existing in the good; in God, that is, as in the exemplar, who is himself the good loving, and so loving the good, from which is every origin of love of the good. Picus is inelegant: 'the motion which is in the first place loving the good', etc. (The editor would read αὐτοκίνητος in place of the printed ἀκίνητος.)

anchorLine: κατὰ τὴν θέσιν βάσεως ἀμετάθετος [male edita, μετάθετος] ἵδρυσις (q).
en: PRIVATIVE BRACKET, p-0708: the printed text has ἀμετάθετος ('unremovable'); the bracket says the earlier edition, badly edited, had μετάθετος ('removable'), without the alpha privative. So the bracket gives a VARIANT that LACKS the privative; the editor's own text keeps ἀ-. It is not a supply and not a deletion by the editor: the editor corrects μετάθετος to ἀμετάθετος, and note (q) confirms ('Quod erat μετάθετος, valde mendosum est').

text: Κατὰ τὴν θέσιν βάσεως ἀμετάθετος ἵδρυσις. Immobilis firmitas et sedes fundati in honesto situs sui, quod maxime justitiæ convenit ; quæ velut terra in hoc universo, suis undique librata momentis, rei ipsum medium immobiliter attendat, ac cuique, quod reipsa illius est, tribuat. Quod erat μετάθετος, valde mendosum est, ac quod aiunt, implicans in adjecto. Picus tamen expedit : Sedem proprii fundamenti translatam in honesto collocat ; si tamen expedire est, sic arbitrarie reddere.
unreadable: in the Greek lemma the letter after ἀ- reads like ἀμετάθετος (printed 'ἀμετάδετος' look) because of the worn type; given as the text prints it
anchorLine: [male edita, μετάθετος] ἵδρυσις (q).
en: 'An unremovable seat according to the position of its base.' Immovable firmness and the seat of what is founded in the honourable placing of itself, which fits justice above all; which, like earth in this universe, poised on all sides by its own moments, attends to the very middle of the thing unmovably, and gives to each what truly is his. What stood in the text, μετάθετος ('removable'), is badly wrong, and, as they say, contradicts itself in the adjective [i.e. the editor restores the privative: ἀμετάθετος]. Picus nonetheless gets out of it: 'He places the seat of his own foundation, transferred, in the honourable'; if indeed this is getting out of it, to render so arbitrarily.

text: Υἱὸν ἀποδειχθῆναι Θεοῦ. Quod deerat vox υἱόν, nihil commodum reddere potuit Picus : ἀπροαίρετον γένεσιν καὶ ὑλικήν, ortum nativitatis non ex libera voluntate et terrenum, quo naturaliter propagamur, ubique Maximus post Greg. Nyss. aliosque Græcos theologos, ex primi parentis transgressione nobis inolevisse docet : alio multiplicandi humani generis modo spiritaliori Deo non ignoto, integra etiam parentum virginitate ; quem August. fatetur se ignorare. Τὸ, ἀπροαίρετον, quod invitam reddit Picus, non satis aptum : sonat enim illa vox contrariam voluntatem et repugnantem, cum vox Græca solum liberæ voluntatis dicat absentiam, oppositione ad spiritalem generationem κατὰ προαίρεσιν ἐν πνεύματι : quæ ex libera voluntate est in spiritu, qua scilicet nascimur a Deo, ut ejus filii simus ac dii Deo similes.
anchorLine: ἀποδειχθῆναι Θεοῦ (r) καὶ Θεὸν κατὰ τὴν χάριν θέσιν,
en: 'To be shown a son of God.' Since the word υἱόν ('son') was missing [in the text], Picus could not render it suitably: 'a not-chosen and material genesis', the origin of a birth not from free will and earthly, by which we are naturally propagated; Maximus everywhere, after Gregory of Nyssa and other Greek theologians, teaches that it grew upon us from the transgression of the first parent, there being another, more spiritual, manner of multiplying the human race, not unknown to God, with the parents' virginity intact; which Augustine confesses he does not know. As for ἀπροαίρετον, which Picus renders 'unwilling' ('invitam'), it is not apt enough: that word sounds like a contrary and resisting will, whereas the Greek word says only the absence of free will, in opposition to the spiritual generation 'by choice in the Spirit': that which is from free will in the Spirit, by which we are born of God, so as to be his sons and gods like God. (The note supplies υἱόν, the missing word, in the text.)

anchorLine: καὶ ἀπροσδεὴς [male edita προσδεής] ὑπάρχων,
en: PRIVATIVE BRACKET, p-0709: the printed text has ἀπροσδεής ('needing nothing'); the bracket says the earlier edition, badly edited, had προσδεής ('needing') without the alpha privative. So the bracket gives a VARIANT that LACKS the privative; the editor's own text keeps ἀ-. It is neither a supply nor a deletion by the editor: he restores ἀπροσδεής and calls προσδεής a misprint. Note (s) is about a different word.

text: Ἐκ περιστάσεως. Cap. sequenti περιστατικὴν ἀνάγκην vocat Maximus necessitatem ex ipsis vitæ mortalis rationibus, ejusque variis casibus ; quam levare artis præceptis studet humana solertia : hæc nempe indigentia, quam idem excludit a primi status felicitate, Καὶ ἀπροσδεὴς ὑπάρχων τῆς περὶ τέχνας περιστατικῆς ἐλεύθερος ἦν. Ubi male Picus, Καὶ προσδεὴς ὑπάρχων· Et cum egeret : quæ ratio est non absolvens ab artium cura, sed potius ei addicens. Alia pridem in aliis non bonis Maximi interpretibus mihi sugillata, unius litteræ seu syllabæ elisione, proclivi lapsu festinantis manus scribæ, decoquentibus quod palam Scripturæ adversetur, ac cujus contrarium Maximo serio adnotetur.
anchorLine: λόγους τεχνῶν ἐκ περιστάσεως (s) διὰ τὴν χρείαν·
en: 'From circumstance.' In the following chapter Maximus calls 'circumstantial necessity' (περιστατικὴν ἀνάγκην) the necessity arising from the very conditions of mortal life and its various chances, which human skill strives to relieve by the precepts of art: namely that indigence which he excludes from the happiness of the first state, 'And being without need (ἀπροσδεής), he was free of the circumstantial need concerning the arts.' Where Picus is wrong with 'Καὶ προσδεὴς ὑπάρχων', 'And when he was in need', a reading that does not release from the care of the arts but rather binds him to it. THE EDITOR, accordingly, KEEPS the privative ἀπροσδεής and treats the other as a slip. I have already pointed out similar [slips] in other not-good interpreters of Maximus: the dropping of one letter or syllable, by the easy lapse of a hasty scribe's hand, making [the passage] contradict Scripture openly, whereas the opposite is seriously noted by Maximus.
